prize_parts.citation: for establishing modern political economics by analysing how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic outcomes

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged: B016, with the same three names. The case is a unified programme that turned the policy outcomes of political systems into an object of formal analysis and evidence. It explains why similar economic conditions lead to different taxation, spending, redistribution and public-goods provision under different electoral rules, constitutional forms and degrees of state capacity. It then takes those implications to cross-country and within-country data. The work is some three decades old and is taught, extended and criticised in public economics, development and political economy, so maturity is not in question. On the chair's overlap question, I think a citation limited to rules, state capacity and fiscal outcomes separates this work from the 2024 prize. That prize concerned the historical origins of institutions and long-run prosperity. This work concerns how specific political rules map into contemporary policy. The trio is a recognisable cut: Persson and Tabellini on constitutions and policy, and Besley with Persson on political agency, accountability and state capacity. I hold this first place with only moderate confidence. Round 1 showed that my reservations about B016 are shared by its own supporters, and that B001 and B020 are serious rivals.
statement.case_against: The reservations are stronger after the exchange. Identification of constitutional and electoral-rule effects is weaker than in design-based candidates such as B019 and B014, because institutions are not randomly assigned. Overlap with 2024 lowers the marginal novelty even if the subjects differ. Credit across the Persson-Tabellini and Besley-Persson strands cannot be cleanly separated, and Persson sits in both, so a three-name cap is a judgment and not a finding. The three first-place files for B016 are not independent evidence, since the chair and I co-author and I have said so. I also see a consistency problem in my own position. If mixed empirical validation counts against B001, as several colleagues argue, then weaker identification must count against B016 by the same standard. I cannot apply one standard to B001 and a softer one to B016. The case for B016 therefore rests on breadth and field-building more than on tested predictions, and I think the committee should say so.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B016 first but concedes that constitutional-effects estimates are largely correlational. He would frame the citation around the analytical framework, notes that later work has moved to better within-country designs, and ranks B019 third for its cleaner identification.
responses.response: I agree with the framing and with the identification concession, and I would use the same wording discipline. I would add a condition. The claim that later within-country designs have sharpened the programme is from recollection, for both of us. The committee should only lean on it if the Scientific Background can point to designs that test predictions of the theory, and not merely related reduced-form facts. If it cannot, the case rests on conceptual breadth alone, and I would then hold B001 more or less level with B016. On B019, I rank it fifth. I respect the credibility of its best designs, but the open attribution questions around Dorn, Katz and the task strand weigh more with me than the identification advantage.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B001 first and B016 second. He keeps B016 behind because of the apportioning problem across three names, contested constitutional identification and adjacency to 2024. His own caveat on B001 is mixed empirical support, and he raises an unverified question about how much novelty lies in the common-agency machinery.
responses.response: The apportionment objection is the one I find hardest to answer. Persson is in both strands, so a trio is defensible but not forced, and a Persson-Tabellini pair would be the narrower fallback. I keep Besley because accountability and state capacity are a distinct and well-developed part of the programme. I accept that this is a judgment call. On B001, your doubt about novelty in the common-agency machinery is one I cannot settle either, since I am working from recollection. I would not treat it as disqualifying, because making that machinery tractable and estimable for trade policy is itself a contribution. We agree on more than the rankings suggest. We both see B001 as the cleaner attribution and B016 as the broader programme, and we differ mainly on how much attribution cleanliness should count.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B020 first and B001 eighth. He treats B001 as primarily theory with mixed confirmation, and argues that B020's selection and reallocation mechanisms are checked against firm-level data in many countries and changed how trade is estimated. He also says the committee should not merge the two Helpman strands.
responses.response: I agree that the two Helpman strands should not be stacked, and I take the chair's question directly. If the committee recognises trade, I could accept either B001 or B020 as a single-part award. B001 is my clearer second choice because of its attribution, with B020 a close third. I do not follow ranking B001 eighth on empirical grounds, though. A framework can earn recognition by making a question answerable. Mixed estimates of protection for sale are what a testable model produces. They are not evidence of failure. That is the same standard I need for B016, and I would apply it to both. Your point about B020's wider footprint in data and estimation is real. It is why B020 has replaced B031 among my alternatives.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B001 first and B016 third. He finds the identification point on B016 the most serious. He argues the strongest cross-country constitutional results remain correlational, whereas B001 makes sharper predictions that can be tested. He also stresses the clean two-person attribution.
responses.response: Part of that comparison I accept. B001's attribution is cleaner, and I have said so. I would qualify the claim that sharper testability favours B001, because you also concede that its empirical record is mixed. A model that makes sharper predictions and then gets mixed confirmation has not clearly beaten a broader programme that makes looser predictions and gets suggestive confirmation. These look to me like different kinds of evidential strength, and I cannot rank one above the other without a common weighting. Your point that your own proximity to political institutions research makes you wary of overweighting B016 is the right disclosure instinct, and I apply the same instinct to myself below.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B020 first. He treats the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as a real risk, but leans towards it not being disqualifying, with moderate confidence. He also recognises Helpman for the firm-heterogeneity work and treats B001 as an alternative. In round 1 he disagreed with my Gertler suggestion on B031.
responses.response: Your answer moves me a little. I said in round 1 that the credit gap was substantial. After the supporters' replies, including Enflo's and Strömberg's, I see it more as a citation-wording problem than a bar. A citation centred on selection and the Melitz-Helpman mechanism is accurate about what it credits. I still think the Scientific Background would need to describe the empirical precursors in full. I do not move B020 above B016 or B001, but it is now my second alternative. On B031, your preference for a Kiyotaki-Moore pair without Gertler is the position I also reached in round 1, so I have dropped B031 from my alternatives. We are frequent co-authors, so my moving towards your view should not be counted as independent confirmation of it.

uncertainties: Whether a citation limited to electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity in fiscal policy separates B016 from the 2024 prize enough, or whether the committee would read it as reducing marginal novelty.
Whether the trio can be defended when the Persson-Tabellini and Besley-Persson strands share Persson, or whether a narrower Persson-Tabellini pair is the more defensible cut.
How to apply one common weighting of identification quality, framework breadth and cumulative field-building to B016, B001, B019 and B020. I have not found one I am confident is neutral across them.
Whether B001's mixed empirical record and B016's weaker identification should be treated as the same kind of limitation, as I argue above, or as different ones.
Whether the B020 attribution gap is workable through citation wording, as the supporters argue, or is a deeper problem.
My assessments of priority, attribution and the later empirical literature rest on recollection and the written openings. I have not independently verified them.
statement.conflict_note: No co-authorship with any credited name on B016, B001 or B020 appears in my supplied profile. I update the disclosure in two ways, both from my own recollection and not from the profile or any independent check. First, I am a Centennial Professor at LSE, and I recall that Timothy Besley, credited on B016, is also at LSE. Second, I recall Torsten Persson, also credited on B016, as long associated with IIES, my home institute at Stockholm University. I know of no collaboration or tie to either of them beyond shared institutions, but this institutional proximity is real, and my first place for B016 should be read with it in mind. My long-standing co-authors Hassler (the chair) and Boppart are committee colleagues, not candidates. Hassler also prefers B016, and Boppart prefers B020 and has not ranked B016 first, so agreement or disagreement with either should not be counted as independent evidence. I am the committee secretary. That is a procedural role and gives me no extra weight on any candidate. These ties are disclosed and not adjudicated.
